newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST - UK jobless to fall sharply again in March.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - UK jobless to fall sharply again in March.

text.p: British unemployment figures for March, due on Wednesday, will almost certainly show another dramatic fall, but economists said huge distortions in the statistics mean the government will get little credit.
"The figures are undoubtedly distorted by the changes that have been made in the calculation of the claimant count," said Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

"The government probably won't get much credit for the recent falls, but then governments often find it hard to get much credit for even genuinely good economic news." A Reuters poll forecast the jobless total fell by 45,000 in March for an unemployment rate of 6.2 percent, unchanged from February. The figures will be released at 0830 GMT on Wednesday.
Most economists agree the monthly data exaggerate the real health of the jobs market.

"There is widespread agreement that the underlying monthly fall in unemployment in recent months has only been about half of the reported fall in the claimant count," said Darshini David, UK economist at HSBC markets, in a recent report.
Even the government, anxious to trumpet any economic success before the May 1 election, has admitted the data exaggerate its employment record.
On the second day of the election campaign, the Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine confessed that only about half of the monthly falls were due to genuine job creation.
"Something like half the reduction that we're seeing is through new jobs," he said after official figures showed a massive 68,200 fall in February.

HSBC's David said if the figures are adjusted to reflect the preponderance of part-time work in the UK and changes made to the claimant criteria by the Conservative administration are stripped out of the equation, the real rate of unemployment could be as high as 14 percent.

"Despite the labour market reforms in the UK in recent years, the extent of unemployment in the UK may not be that different than in France and Germany despite the claims of the official figures," she said in a recent report on unemployment.
But with real falls of around 30,000 a month, the labour market is clearly benefiting from the economic upturn and new jobs are being created.
Economists say the March report is likely to show a higher increase in job centre vacancies than February's 7,800 and favourable recruitment intentions in the services sector in particular.

But the effect of this labour market tightening has already been felt and average earnings data also due on Wednesday should show wage pressures continue to build. Underlying annual average earnings picked up to 5.0 percent in January compared with an upwardly revised figure of 4.75 percent in December. The first estimate of December's earnings was 4.25 percent. The Reuters poll forecasts average earnings growth may slow to 4.75 percent again in February.

"The rise in average earnings in January may have been exaggerated by bonus payments in the financial services sector," said David Mackie, UK economist at JP Morgan. "Nevertheless, the upward trend in earnings growth has been evidence for the last eighteen months since service sector firms have reported difficulty in recruiting appropriate skilled labour."
